The house on Alder Street had been empty for eleven years before Marta finally pushed open the gate and walked up the path. The solicitor had sent her a single page, folded twice, that said the property was hers and that the keys were with the neighbour. She read it again on the step, then put it away. The document told her nothing she wanted to know. She had come for the letters, if there were letters, and for the smell of the hallway that she remembered as a child, and for the cover of the old piano that her grandmother had kept closed so the keys would not yellow.

Mrs. Adler from next door came out with the keys on a ring the size of a small wheel, and stood with her while the lock turned. She said the roof had been patched twice and that the gutters needed clearing before winter. Marta nodded and asked about the garden, and Mrs. Adler said the roses had gone wild and that the apple tree still gave fruit, though nobody picked it.

Inside, the air was cold and dry. Dust covered the stairs in a pale film, and the light through the front window showed the shape of the furniture that was no longer there. Marta went through the rooms one at a time, opening cupboards, closing them, listening to the floorboards. In the study she found a box of papers under the window and sat down on the floor to go through it. There were receipts, an old passport, a folded map of a country that no longer existed under that name, and a stack of newsletters from a birding society that her grandmother had never once mentioned. Marta read a few of them and laughed out loud at a complaint about the price of seed.

She worked through the box until the room grew dark. Somewhere above her a door moved, though no one was upstairs, and she told herself it was the wind. She thought about the archive in the city, the building with the green lamps where she had spent a month of her twenties reading other people's letters, and how she had always believed that a thing written down was a thing that could be saved. It was a comforting idea and she had never quite given it up, even after the archive flooded, even after the boxes came back stained and unreadable and the staff apologised in a letter that ran to two pages.

When she finally stood, her knees ached. She carried the box to the car and locked the house, and on the step she turned and looked back at the front window, where the dust she had disturbed was still turning slowly in the last of the light. Mrs. Adler had left a note on the gatepost, written in a careful, upright hand, with a number to call about the roof. Marta read it twice. The cover of the piano stayed closed, and she thought that was probably right.
